evidence: The speaker says an employer will deduct tax from what a student earns. Pay may be weekly or monthly, and insurance contributions depend on the employer and circumstances.
why: Tax is explicitly deducted from earnings, so option A is the only statement presented as generally applicable.
trap: B: Payment may be weekly or monthly, so weekly pay is not guaranteed. C: Insurance contributions are only a possibility and are not described as compulsory private insurance.
explanation: The definite point is that tax is deducted from earnings; payment frequency and insurance arrangements can vary.

evidence: The speaker specifically advises students who decide to leave a job to put their notice in writing. Email is not used by every employer, and a mobile phone is mentioned only as a practical way to contact an employer.
why: Putting the decision to leave in writing is explicit advice, which matches option A.
trap: B: The speaker warns that not all employers use email. C: Having a mobile phone is treated as useful for communication, not as the main formal advice.
explanation: The formal recommendation is to give notice in writing when leaving the job.

prompt: According to the speaker, a part-time job can

options.text: lead to a full-time job after graduation.
provide a useful work record for the future.
give the chance to develop team-work skills.

evidence: The speaker says part-time work helps build an employment record that reflects a student's skills and capabilities, and that evidence of such work on a CV can give graduates an advantage.
why: Building an employment record for later applications directly matches option B.
trap: A: A part-time job may help later applications, but the speaker does not promise it will become a full-time job after graduation. C: The speaker mentions several useful skills, but the main point here is the value of the employment record itself.
explanation: Part-time work gives students documented experience that can strengthen future job applications.

prompt: How did John choose the topic of his research project?

options.text: He thought the information would be useful for town planning.
He has a special interest in the use of public services.
He read about a similar study which had been done earlier.

evidence: John says he found a report in the college library about an investigation carried out ten years earlier and thought it would be interesting to do a parallel study.
why: The earlier report gave him the idea for the project, so option C is correct.
trap: A: The tutor says the information could be useful for town planning, but John does not say this is why he chose the topic. B: John explicitly says he has no special interest in public services.
explanation: John chose the topic after reading about a similar investigation from ten years earlier.

prompt: During his research, John is expecting to find that

options.text: the use of public services has altered very little.
a group of people has changed its habits.
the most frequently used facility is the library.

evidence: John predicts changes in patterns of use, including older people using the sports centre more often, while he expects use of the library to have decreased.
why: That prediction means a particular group - older people - has changed its habits, which matches option B.
trap: A: John expects noticeable changes rather than very little change. C: He expects library use to have fallen, so he does not predict that the library is the most frequently used facility.
explanation: John expects the earlier pattern of public-service use to have changed, especially among older users.
